cards.question: Why is npos not an ordinary index?
cards.answer: It is the library’s absence result. Treating it as a location or performing arithmetic on it does not establish a valid substring boundary.

cards.question: Why use a local candidate?
cards.answer: It delays mutation of caller-owned state until all validation succeeds. That makes failure behavior predictable and testable.

cards.question: Why can a string view be safe here?
cards.answer: The owning string remains alive and unchanged for the parser call. The view does not escape beyond that lifetime.

cards.question: Why distinguish grammar from range?
cards.answer: Text can be syntactically numeric while representing an invalid identifier. Each boundary rejects a different class of input.

cards.question: What does std::string own?
cards.answer: It owns its character sequence and manages its storage. A string object can grow; a borrowed character pointer is not the same ownership boundary.

cards.question: How do += and assignment differ for a string?
cards.answer: += appends to existing text. Assignment replaces the existing sequence with the supplied text.

cards.question: What does string::size() count?
cards.answer: It counts char elements. For UTF-8 text, that is not necessarily the number of human-perceived characters.

cards.question: What does find return when the requested text is absent?
cards.answer: std::string::npos. Check that absence marker before treating the result as a valid position.

cards.question: Why can adding one to npos create a wrong substring calculation?
cards.answer: npos is an absence marker, not a found index. Arithmetic on it does not turn a failed search into a valid delimiter location.

cards.question: How does substr(position, count) interpret count?
cards.answer: It is the requested number of characters, not an ending index. The result is limited by the remaining sequence; an out-of-range starting position throws.

cards.question: How does operator>> into a string differ from getline?
cards.answer: Formatted extraction reads a whitespace-delimited word. getline reads up to its delimiter, allowing spaces inside the line.

cards.question: Why can getline read an empty line just after reading a number?
cards.answer: The formatted read can leave the newline in the stream. getline then consumes that newline immediately. Handle the transition deliberately.

cards.question: What two results from from_chars must a strict integer parser check?
cards.answer: Check the error code and the returned pointer. Success without reaching the field's end can mean only a numeric prefix was parsed.

cards.question: Does from_chars skip leading spaces in this integer use?
cards.answer: No. It follows its specified numeric format rather than the stream's whitespace rules. Decide whether trimming belongs in your input contract.

cards.question: Why parse into a temporary before updating saved state?
cards.answer: A rejected field can then leave the prior value unchanged. Commit only after representation and domain checks succeed.

cards.question: How can a string edit invalidate a borrowed character pointer?
cards.answer: An edit may reallocate storage. Reacquire the pointer after the edit and do not assume old addresses still refer to live characters.

cards.question: What must bool parseField(const std::string& text, int& output) accept and reject?
